title: SMTP Service Extension for Authentication
summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a client name an authentication mechanism, run an authentication exchange with the server, and optionally set up a security layer for the rest of the session. It works by profiling the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) for SMTP. It replaces RFC 2554.

plainLanguage.summary: Before a mail server lets you send mail, it can ask for a password-like proof that you are really you. This explains how that check works.

questions: what is the smtp auth command
which sasl mechanism must smtp support
what does auth=<> mean in mail from
subtitle: How an SMTP client proves who it is to a mail server, using SASL mechanisms and a new AUTH command.

tldr.problem: Plain SMTP has no way for a client to prove its identity to the server, so servers cannot tell who is submitting mail.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises an AUTH keyword listing SASL mechanisms in its EHLO reply. The client then sends an AUTH command, runs a challenge and response exchange encoded in base64, and may also negotiate a security layer.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2554 and makes SASL PLAIN over TLS mandatory to implement. RFC 5248 has since updated it.

today: RFC 4954 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2554. It has been updated by RFC 5248 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
RFC 4954 defines an SMTP service extension named "Authentication". With it, a client can name an authentication mechanism, run an exchange with the server, and optionally negotiate a security layer for the rest of the session. It is a profile of the Simple Authentication and Security Layer (SASL) for SMTP.

The server announces the extension with the EHLO keyword AUTH, followed by a space-separated list of the SASL mechanisms it offers. That list MAY change after a successful STARTTLS. The extension adds a new verb, AUTH, and an optional AUTH parameter on MAIL FROM. The RFC says it is appropriate for the message submission protocol too.

It obsoletes RFC 2554. Compared to that RFC, it deprecates the 538 response code, adds a new Enhanced Status Code, requires support for the SASLprep profile for authorization identities, and clarifies how AUTH works with SMTP PIPELINING.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail server tells you which secret-handshake styles it knows. You pick one and use it to show you are allowed in.

sections.title: The AUTH Command and Its Exchange
sections.content:
The command is AUTH mechanism [initial-response]. The client names a SASL mechanism and the server runs that mechanism's exchange. After one AUTH succeeds, no more AUTH commands may be issued in the session, and the server MUST reject them with a 503 reply. AUTH is also not allowed during a mail transaction, and a server MUST reject it with a 503 reply there too. If the mechanism is not supported, or requires an encryption layer, the server rejects the command with a 504 reply.

A server challenge is a 334 reply whose text is only the base64-encoded challenge. A client response is a line of base64. To cancel, the client sends a line with a single asterisk (*), and the server MUST reject the AUTH with a 501 reply. A challenge with no data is a 334 reply with no text, written as 334 with the trailing space.

The optional initial response saves a round trip for mechanisms where the client speaks first. If the initial response would be zero length, the client sends a single = instead. If the command would exceed the SMTP line length limit, the client MUST NOT use an initial response. Everything must be strict base64: invalid characters, or a pad character anywhere but the end, MUST be rejected. Clients and servers MUST handle long lines, and the RFC notes that 12288 octets was considered sufficient at the time of writing.

On success the server sends 235. If it cannot authenticate the client it SHOULD send 535 unless a more specific code fits.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard says something in code, you reply in code, and you go back and forth until the guard says yes or no. You can walk away at any time by saying a single star.

sections.title: Mechanisms, Layers and Pipelining
sections.content:
To ensure interoperability, clients and servers MUST implement the PLAIN SASL mechanism running over TLS (see RFC 4616 and RFC 3207). Many deployed implementations also use CRAM-MD5, so new implementations MAY implement it, but the RFC warns that it gives no server authentication.

A server MUST offer a configuration that does not permit plaintext password mechanisms unless STARTTLS has been negotiated or some other protection against password snooping is in place. If a security layer is negotiated, it takes effect right after the CRLF that ends the last client response (for the server, after the CRLF of its success reply). The SMTP session then resets to its initial state, both sides MUST discard what they learned before, and the client SHOULD send EHLO next. If TLS and a SASL layer are both active, TLS encoding is applied after SASL encoding.

With PIPELINING, AUTH MUST be the last command in a pipelined group. The exception is an AUTH with an initial response for a one-round-trip mechanism such as PLAIN or EXTERNAL when no security layer is negotiated. The SASL service name is smtp, and it is also used for the submission protocol.

If an AUTH command fails, the client MAY continue without authentication, try another mechanism, or present different credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: Some secret handshakes are safe to say out loud only in a soundproof room. The server must be able to refuse them unless the room is soundproof, which is what TLS provides.

sections.title: The AUTH Parameter on MAIL FROM
sections.content:
The extension also adds AUTH=mailbox to the MAIL FROM command. It carries the mailbox of whoever submitted the message, or <> when that is unknown or not sufficiently authenticated. The mailbox is encoded as an xtext, and the parameter extends the maximum MAIL FROM line length by 500 characters.

It lets cooperating servers in a trusted environment pass along who originally submitted a message. A server that trusts the client's authenticated identity SHOULD pass the same mailbox on when relaying to another server that supports AUTH. Because of this, a server advertising the extension MUST accept the parameter even when the client has not authenticated.

If the server does not trust the client enough, or the client is not authenticated, it MUST behave as if AUTH=<> was supplied, and it MUST then send AUTH=<> when relaying to any server it authenticated to. A server MAY treat mailing list expansion as a new submission. The RFC notes that an implementation that parses and discards every AUTH parameter and always sends AUTH=<> still complies.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like writing on a parcel who first handed it in. If the post office does not trust that name, it writes "unknown" instead.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
The RFC defines reply codes with suggested enhanced status codes for authentication results. The ones with a client action attached matter most: on 535 the client SHOULD ask the user for new credentials, on 454 (temporary failure) it SHOULD NOT prompt for another password, and on 534 (mechanism too weak) it SHOULD retry with a new mechanism.

The 530 reply SHOULD be returned by any command other than AUTH, EHLO, HELO, NOOP, RSET or QUIT when server policy requires authentication and none is in force. The 538 code is documented only for historical purposes. Modern servers SHOULD NOT advertise mechanisms that are not allowed without encryption, unless sufficient encryption is in use.

Servers also add a requirement for trace headers: after a successful authentication, a server SHOULD use the ESMTPA or ESMTPSA keyword in the "with" clause of the Received header field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each number is a short answer from the server, like "come in", "try again later", or "wrong password". The client knows what to do from the number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Everything before the SASL negotiation is in the clear and can be changed by an active attacker. That is why both sides MUST discard what they learned before a security layer starts. A client that wants an encrypted tunnel should be configured to never send mail to that server when the connection is not mutually authenticated and encrypted. Otherwise an attacker could hijack the connection and pretend the server lacks the extension, or make every AUTH fail.

Servers MAY drop the connection after failed attempts, but SHOULD NOT do so until at least 3 attempts have failed. An implementation that supports mechanisms open to eavesdropping, such as PLAIN, MUST support at least one configuration where they are not advertised or used without an external security layer such as TLS.

The RFC says this extension does not replace end-to-end signing or encryption such as S/MIME or PGP. It is generally useful only within a trusted enclave, protects the whole envelope, and authenticates the submission rather than the authorship of the content.

For PLAIN over TLS, the client verifies the server certificate and checks the hostname it used to connect against the certificate. If either check fails, the client MUST NOT authenticate with PLAIN.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not whisper your password until you are sure you are in a private room talking to the right person. If you cannot check, do not say it.
